title: Labels and the table
subtitle: Reading Champagne and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: A Champagne label shows the house or grower, the sweetness level, the producer code, NV or a vintage, and sometimes Grand Cru, Premier Cru, Blanc de Blancs or Blanc de Noirs. The word Champagne itself is protected: only wine from the region made by the traditional method can use it.

steps.title: Serving
steps.body: Serve at 8 to 10 degrees; vintage and prestige cuvées a little warmer. A white wine glass shows the aromas better than a narrow flute. Open by holding the cork and turning the bottle slowly, letting the pressure out with a sigh, not a pop.
steps.highlight: 8 to 10 degrees, in a wine glass

steps.prompt: Why might a white wine glass suit Champagne better than a flute?
options: It lets aromas gather and show
steps.explanation: A wider bowl reveals the wine's aromas.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Brut Champagne suits oysters, caviar, sushi, fried food and salty snacks; acidity and bubbles cut fat and salt. Blanc de Blancs suits shellfish; Blanc de Noirs and rosé suit poultry, salmon and charcuterie. Vintage and aged Champagne suit truffle and roast chicken. Demi-Sec suits fruit desserts.

steps.explanation: Sweet cake makes Brut taste sour; choose Demi-Sec.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show producer, dosage, code and vintage
Serve at 8 to 10 degrees in a wine glass
Brut suits oysters and fried food; Demi-Sec suits desserts
